title: Sisig
description: Boiled-then-grilled pork, finely chopped and tossed with onions, chili and calamansi, served sizzling on a hot plate — a Kapampangan beer-hall favorite turned everyday main.

ingredients.item: pork belly and pork ears, mixed for texture
ingredients.note: or use pork belly only if ears aren't available
reduce or omit for a milder batch
optional, cracked on top while sizzling

steps: Combine pork, vinegar, soy sauce, garlic, peppercorns, bay leaves and salt in a pot with enough water to cover. Bring to a boil, skimming scum, then simmer 45-60 minutes until tender.
Drain well and grill or broil the pork for 8-10 minutes per side until charred and crisp at the edges.
Let cool slightly, then chop the meat finely into small bits.
In a bowl, combine chopped meat, onion, chili peppers, calamansi juice and liquid seasoning; mix well.
Season with salt and pepper to taste.
Transfer to a preheated sizzling plate, top with a raw egg if using, and serve immediately with rice.
tips: Don't skip the char on the grill — it's what gives sisig its signature crisp bite, not just the boiling.
Preheat the sizzling plate on the stovetop for a few minutes before serving so it actually sizzles at the table.
kidNote: Sisig is properly spicy and uses pig ears and cheek, a texture kids often reject — set aside a plain portion made from just the pork belly meat, skip the chilies, and mix it with a little calamansi and soy sauce instead.
nutritionNote: Rich in protein but very high in saturated fat from the pork and any added mayonnaise; balance with a big side of steamed rice and a cucumber-tomato salad.

title: Crispy Pata
description: A whole pork leg boiled until tender, dried, then deep-fried until the skin blisters into crackling — a party centerpiece served with a soy-vinegar dip.

ingredients.note: optional, omit for the kids' bowl

steps: Combine pata, water, onion, garlic, peppercorns, bay leaves and salt in a large pot; bring to a boil.
Lower heat, cover, and simmer 60-75 minutes until the meat is fork-tender, skimming scum as needed.
Drain well and pat completely dry, then refrigerate uncovered for at least 1 hour (or overnight) so the skin dries out.
Heat oil in a deep, heavy pot to 175°C (350°F).
Carefully lower the pata into the hot oil and fry 12-15 minutes, basting hot oil over the top and turning once, until deep golden and blistered.
Drain on a rack, rest 5 minutes, then chop into serving pieces.
Mix soy sauce, vinegar, diced onion and chili for the dipping sauce.
Serve hot with rice and the dipping sauce.
tips: Drying the boiled pata before frying is what makes the skin blister and crackle instead of staying chewy.
Use a tall, heavy pot and a splatter screen — the oil spits when the pata goes in.
nutritionNote: Very high in fat from the skin and deep-frying; treat it as an occasional treat and serve with a vinegar-forward dip and a big vegetable side to balance the plate.

title: Dinuguan
description: Pork belly simmered in vinegar and pork blood until the sauce turns thick and dark, tangy and savory with a touch of chili — the Philippines' 'chocolate meat' stew.

ingredients.note: ask your butcher for fresh pork blood, sold at wet markets
mild heat; add a bird's eye chili for more kick

steps: Stir 2 tablespoons of the vinegar into the pork blood and set aside.
Heat oil in a pot; sauté onion, garlic and ginger until softened.
Add pork belly and cook, stirring occasionally, until lightly browned.
Add fish sauce and cook 1-2 minutes.
Pour in the remaining vinegar; boil uncovered without stirring for 3-5 minutes to cook off the raw acidity.
Add water, cover, and simmer 15-20 minutes until the pork is tender.
Stir in the pork blood, mixing well to prevent lumps, and simmer gently until the sauce thickens.
Add brown sugar and chili; simmer 10 minutes more, then season with salt and pepper. Serve hot with rice or puto.
tips: Don't stir while the vinegar cooks off — it needs a few uncovered minutes to lose its raw sharpness.
The sauce needs no cornstarch; the blood's protein thickens it naturally once heated through.
kidNote: This is a blood-based stew that most young kids find strange in both look and taste — set aside a plain portion of the pork belly before adding the blood if they want to try it, and leave the chili out of their bowl.
nutritionNote: High in iron from the blood but also high in saturated fat from the pork belly; serve smaller portions with plenty of steamed rice and a vinegar-dressed vegetable side.

title: Binagoongang Baboy
description: Pork belly braised with tomatoes, shrimp paste and chilies into a deeply savory, faintly funky stew — a weeknight favorite best eaten with fried eggplant and rice.

ingredients.note: omit if your shrimp paste is already sweetened

steps: Heat oil in a wide pan; cook pork cubes until browned and the fat renders.
Add onion and garlic; cook until softened.
Stir in shrimp paste and cook about 1 minute.
Add tomatoes, mashing with the back of a spoon until softened and juicy.
Pour in vinegar; simmer uncovered without stirring for 2-4 minutes.
Add water, chilies and sugar; stir to combine.
Lower heat, cover, and simmer until the pork is fork-tender and the sauce is reduced.
Season with salt and pepper; serve hot with fried eggplant and rice.
tips: Sauté raw shrimp paste a little longer, until it darkens, to tame its fishy edge.
Commercial sautéed bagoong is already sweet, so taste before adding extra sugar.
kidNote: The shrimp paste gives this dish a strong savory-funky smell kids can be wary of, and the chilies add real heat — spoon out plain pork and sauce for the kids before stirring in extra chili, and pan-fry a few slices of eggplant on the side.
nutritionNote: Pork belly and shrimp paste make this rich in sodium and fat; balance with steamed rice, fried eggplant, and a side of fresh tomato for fibre.

title: Bulalo
description: Beef shanks and marrow bones simmered low and slow into a clear, deeply savory broth with corn and pechay — the classic cold-weather soup from Batangas and Tagaytay.

ingredients.item: corn on the cob, husked and halved

steps: Combine beef shanks and cold water in a large pot; bring to a boil, then drain and rinse the meat to remove impurities.
Return the meat to the pot with fresh cold water to cover; bring to a boil, skimming off scum.
Add onion, fish sauce and peppercorns; lower heat, cover, and simmer 1.5-2 hours until the meat is fork-tender.
Add corn and simmer 10-15 minutes until tender.
Add pechay and green onions; cook 2-3 minutes until just wilted.
Season with salt to taste.
Serve hot with rice and a side dip of fish sauce and calamansi juice.
tips: Starting with cold water and parboiling the meat first keeps the broth clear instead of cloudy.
Keep the pot at a bare simmer, not a rolling boil, so the broth doesn't turn murky.
nutritionNote: A protein-rich broth soup; the marrow bone adds richness, so balance with extra vegetables and go light on rice if watching saturated fat.

title: Chicken Afritada
description: Chicken braised in a fresh tomato sauce with potatoes, carrots and bell peppers until tender — a mild, colorful stew found at family lunches across the Philippines.
steps: Heat oil in a pan; brown potatoes and carrots, then remove and set aside.
Quickly sauté bell peppers, then remove and set aside.
Sauté onion and garlic until softened; add chicken and brown lightly.
Add tomatoes and mash until softened and juicy; stir in fish sauce.
Add water, bring to a boil, then lower heat, cover, and simmer 15-25 minutes until chicken is tender.
Return potatoes and carrots to the pan; cook until fork-tender.
Add bell peppers and peas; cook 1-2 minutes until just tender.
Season with salt and pepper; simmer until the sauce reaches your desired thickness. Serve hot with rice.
tips: Pan-frying the potatoes and carrots first keeps them from falling apart during the long simmer.
Cut everything into similar sizes so it all finishes cooking together.
nutritionNote: A balanced one-pan meal with protein and vegetables already built in; go easy on the oil used for browning and serve with plain rice to keep it lighter.

title: Beef Tapa
description: Thin beef strips cured overnight in soy sauce, calamansi and garlic, then pan-seared until caramelized — the beef half of a classic tapsilog breakfast plate.
steps: Combine soy sauce, calamansi juice, garlic, sugar, salt and pepper in a non-reactive bowl; stir until dissolved.
Add beef and massage to coat fully; cover and refrigerate overnight to cure.
Drain the beef from the marinade.
Heat a little oil in a wide pan over medium heat; add beef in a single layer.
Cook, turning occasionally, 3-5 minutes until the liquid the meat releases is nearly absorbed.
Add a little more oil and continue cooking until the meat is browned and caramelized.
Remove from pan, slice into serving portions, and serve hot with garlic fried rice and a fried egg.
tips: The overnight marinate (about 8 hours, unattended in the fridge) is what cures the beef properly — don't skip it, but don't go past 24 hours or the acid turns the texture mushy.
Freeze the beef for a few minutes before slicing to make thin, even cuts easier.
nutritionNote: A good lean-protein breakfast option; pair with extra vegetables or a side salad since the usual accompaniments — garlic rice and a fried egg — are already calorie-dense.

title: Paksiw na Isda
description: Whole fish gently simmered in vinegar, garlic and ginger with a touch of bitter gourd and chili — a tangy, no-fuss everyday dish that keeps well overnight.

ingredients.item: whole fish (tilapia, bangus or pompano), cleaned

ingredients.note: optional; omit for a milder, less bitter dish

steps: Combine vinegar and water in a wide pan; add salt and peppercorns and bring to a boil.
Arrange the fish in the pan along with the ginger, garlic, onion, bitter gourd and chili.
Cover and simmer over low to medium heat for 12-15 minutes until the fish is cooked through.
Turn off the heat and transfer carefully to a serving plate.
Serve hot with steamed rice.
tips: Don't stir once the fish is in the pan — gently shake the pan instead to keep the fillets from breaking apart.
Leftovers taste even better the next day once the vinegar mellows.
kidNote: This is a sour, vinegar-forward dish, and the bitter gourd adds real bitterness — leave the bitter gourd out of the kids' portion and give them a piece of fish spooned with a little extra broth rather than straight vinegar sauce.
nutritionNote: A light, low-fat way to eat fish since the vinegar base needs little added oil; pair with rice and a cooked green vegetable for a complete meal.

title: Ginataang Gulay
description: A creamy coconut-milk vegetable stew loaded with eggplant, squash, green beans and jackfruit, given body with a little pork and shrimp — best with a big pot of rice.

ingredients.note: or use fish sauce for a milder flavor

ingredients.item: young green jackfruit, cut into chunks

steps: Heat oil in a wide pan; sauté onion and garlic until softened.
Add pork and cook until lightly browned.
Add shrimp and cook just until it turns pink.
Stir in shrimp paste and cook 1-2 minutes.
Pour in coconut milk and simmer 3-5 minutes until slightly thickened.
Add jackfruit and cook 3-5 minutes.
Add kalabasa and cook until tender but still holding its shape.
Add green beans and eggplant; cook until the vegetables are tender and the sauce has thickened.
Season with salt and pepper; serve hot with rice.
tips: If using fresh jackfruit instead of canned or frozen, add a little extra coconut milk since it takes longer to soften.
Cut the vegetables into similar sizes so they finish cooking together.
nutritionNote: Coconut milk makes this high in saturated fat, so serve modest portions alongside plain rice; the eggplant, squash, beans and jackfruit give it good fibre for a vegetable-forward main.

title: Adobong Kangkong
description: Water spinach braised adobo-style with pork belly in vinegar and soy sauce — a quick, budget-friendly way to get greens onto the table alongside grilled or fried fish.

ingredients.item: kangkong (water spinach), trimmed and cut into 3-inch lengths
pork belly, cut into thin strips

steps: Wash the kangkong, keeping the sturdier stalks separate from the leaves.
Heat oil in a wide skillet; sauté onion and garlic until softened.
Add pork and cook until lightly browned.
Add vinegar and boil uncovered without stirring for 2-3 minutes.
Add soy sauce and water; bring to a boil.
Lower heat, cover, and simmer 8-10 minutes until the pork is tender and the sauce is reduced.
Raise the heat to high, add the kangkong stalks and cook 1-2 minutes.
Add the kangkong leaves and cook, stirring, about 1 minute until just wilted.
Season with salt and pepper; serve hot with rice.
tips: Add the stalks before the leaves since they need a little longer to soften.
Don't overcook the kangkong — pull it off the heat as soon as the leaves wilt, since residual heat keeps cooking it.
kidNote: The vinegar makes this a fairly sour dish — serve the sauce on the side for picky kids and let them spoon on only as much as they like, rather than starting with a very saucy bowl.
nutritionNote: Kangkong is a good source of iron and fibre; the pork belly adds richness, so use a smaller amount or swap in a leaner cut if serving this often.
